sources.notes: The original NYC DSA newsletter archive explicitly labels issue16 Monday, June05,2017 in paragraph7 and identifies the named candidate's email interview in paragraph26. The2022 Substack migration notice is sitewide publisher text, not a2017 candidate statement or a claim of a particular article-revision date. Only the candidate's explicitly prefixed answers are reviewed; surrounding newsletter stories are not his words.

statements.claim: Supports strengthening landlord accountability while building affordable homes for displaced residents, whom he says should not be victimized again.
Makes preserving parking a stated condition for supporting Citi Bike in the district; separately criticizes subway reliability.
Argues that private-street residents pay taxes and deserve garbage collection, and proposes restoring bulk collection or improving public outreach about arrangements.

Explicitly opposes supervised injection facilities and favors counseling, treatment, recreation and family engagement. This2017 position is not inferred from his endorsement and is not presented as medical advice.
Supports counseling and treatment facilities as part of the opioid response. This affirmative proposition is distinct from his separate rejection of supervised injection facilities.
Presents his candidacy as community leadership, inclusion and resistance to threats against immigrants and civil liberties.
Proposes working with state-level colleagues for single-payer healthcare; does not claim a council member can enact the state program alone.

statements.quote: municipal voting for green card holders
statements.claim: Supports municipal voting for green-card holders. This records a2017 policy proposal, not current election eligibility instructions.
Wants community boards elected rather than appointed.

statements.quote: closing Rikers in under ten years
statements.claim: Supports closing Rikers in less than ten years, as stated in2017.

Explains seeking DSA support through an anti-inequality and justice agenda independent of the political establishment. Elsewhere in the interview he also affirms working across party lines, so this is not coded as rejecting all compromise.
Proposes using fines on exploiting landlords to fund relocation of tenants, while exploring whether some unsafe units could be made safe and lawful.
Favors waterfront/pier bike share for recreation while doubting its transportation utility in this district. This is limited support, not opposition to every bike-share installation.

statements.quote: deserve to have their garbage picked up
statements.claim: Supports collection for taxpaying private-street residents and presents participation in their lawsuit as his chosen route.
Promises a new school within four years to address overcrowding.
Explicitly opposes charter schools and argues they are unnecessary in a district with strong public schools.
Favors prevention, reducing stigma and education for children. The reporter's separate summary of his injection-site position is not promoted to a literal candidate quotation.
Describes municipal problem-solving and constituent service as a direct form of activism, not simply a party-establishment identity.
Proposes a court process using evidence and resident complaints to authorize inspections of illegal conversions; census and fiscal claims remain attributed.
Supports bringing Citi Bike into community boards10 and11 with public participation in choosing locations.

statements.quote: If a street is not mapped
statements.claim: Declines to force city trucks down unmapped private streets and instead proposes curbside disposal under those conditions.
Withholds charter-school support unless schools accept all children equally and permit employees to join unions. His claims about current charter practices are not independently verified.

Supports the existing counseling center and broader access, and cautions against evaluating one study expense without the whole government picture. This does not establish his support for supervised injection facilities.
Presents himself as a moderate able to work across party lines and independently of party leadership.
Argues fines alone can displace residents and favors more affordable housing to provide alternatives to unsafe conversions.
Sees congestion benefits from bike share but calls for resident consultation, safety instruction and careful siting around parking constraints.
Supports collection for private-street taxpayers and proposes smaller trucks as the practical remedy.
Prefers extending existing schools as a faster response to crowding than waiting for entirely new buildings; this is not opposition to public education.
Opposes supervised injection facilities and favors treatment/education and enforcement against suppliers.
Emphasizes service and personal door-knocking rather than frequent press releases; this describes her stated approach, not independently measured campaign activity.

comparisons.analysis: Both connect unsafe conversions to affordability and tenant protection. El-Yateem foregrounds affordable construction and stronger accountability; Brannan specifies a relocation fund financed by landlord fines. These tools can coexist.

El-Yateem specifies affordable replacement housing alongside accountability; Carroll specifies judicially authorized inspections. The selected answers do not establish that either rejects the other's measure.
Both explicitly propose more affordable homes for people otherwise displaced from unsafe conversions and reject treating fines alone as a sufficient remedy.

El-Yateem conditions bike-share support on preserving parking; Brannan favors waterfront recreation while doubting transportation utility. Both have qualified positions, not a simple pro-bike versus anti-bike split.
El-Yateem emphasizes a no-parking-loss condition; Carroll emphasizes community participation in siting. These requirements are not inherently incompatible.

Both raise parking and siting concerns. El-Yateem makes retaining parking an explicit condition; Tong additionally emphasizes resident polling and rider safety. Her question about siting is not silently converted into an identical veto.
Both argue taxpaying private-street residents deserve garbage collection. Brannan emphasizes litigation while El-Yateem describes service restoration and public outreach.
Both support garbage collection for private-street taxpayers; Tong specifies smaller trucks as a practical tool.

El-Yateem argues for collection based on taxpayer status. Carroll explicitly declines truck access while a street remains unmapped and proposes curbside disposal instead. This is a stated condition on service rather than an invented general opposition to sanitation.

Both explicitly oppose supervised injection facilities in these2017 interviews and favor counseling or treatment. The DSA endorsement is not used to infer the reverse position, and these statements are not clinical recommendations.
Both affirm counseling and treatment resources. This agreement is limited to that tool: Carroll's quoted answer does not establish agreement with El-Yateem's separate opposition to injection sites.

El-Yateem foregrounds counseling, treatment and family engagement; Brannan foregrounds prevention, stigma reduction and child education. No direct injection-site disagreement is coded because Brannan's position on that detail appears only in reporter paraphrase here.

El-Yateem foregrounds inclusion and resistance to attacks on civil liberties; Carroll presents a moderate cross-party community representative. This does not imply El-Yateem refuses cross-party cooperation; his separate email interview explicitly endorses it.

El-Yateem foregrounds inclusive community leadership and civil-liberties resistance; Brannan describes municipal constituent service as activism. The evidence does not support labeling Brannan simply anti-activist.

El-Yateem foregrounds inclusion and civil-liberties leadership; Tong foregrounds constituent work and personal outreach over publicity. These are stated emphases, not measurements of how much either campaign advertised.
